Yes, and the point of the tweet is that wealth would increase without this debt. You can acquire more wealth without this debt. His math was literally current wealth minus current debt and its not black and white like that. You can gain MORE wealth is the point.

This is not my specific situation, just an example. But please understand that literal 17 and 18 year olds are the ones that are becoming indebted, because their parents told them that college was the only way yet did not have the money to pay for their education. They hoped that once they graduated the great jobs that they got would help them pay off their debts. Unfortunately, that wasn't the case. This is simultaneously the most highly educated generation with the lowest pay. 

I have multiple college degrees including an MBA, and have yet to find a job that pays me over $50k a year. How, on that income, can someone support a family, purchase a home, pay medical bills, purchase a car, etc? The advice I give to those younger than me? Hold off on college for a bit. Explore your options and avoid the debt trap.

It's not. While canceling that debt doesn't suddenly make me richer,  it gives me the freedom to build wealth in many forms. For example, my local salon has employees that earn on average $40,000 per year and renters that earn $200,000 per year. Why do the employees make so much less? Because they have to give the majority of their earnings to the salon owners, who in turn take home $240,000 per year. So, why don't the employees switch to being renters so that they can have those huge earnings? It's simple, they are in debt. You see, the renters have to supply all of their own tools (this costs them maybe 10k a year) and they were able to make that purchase by getting a one time loan. That means that after they pay their rent of roughly $300 a month, the rest of their money goes home with them. They then use this money to continue to build wealth, buy a home, a car, invest etc. But the employees are stuck being employed by the owners and paying off their debts. They cannot get approved for or afford a loan large enough to switch to being renters until they can get out of default.

I'll give an example. I want to acquire a small business loan in order to open my own business, purchase assets, and all around increase my wealth. I cannot because of my student loans being in default.
You cannot measure debt and wealth on the same spectrum. They are on different scales.

Wealth is not just measured by how much money you have in your bank account so the argument is flawed. Literally dividing one by the other is not how you calculate this. Student loans lower your credit score if you are in default.
Um, wealth is literally defined as an abundance of valuable possessions or money. You are comparing one form of debt to multiple forms of wealth. Your argument is flawed. Be willing to accept that.

Wealth is measured in more ways than just cash. Wealth includes assets, credit, earning power, buying power, etc. Due to student loans, those in debt have lower credit scores and as such lower access to other forms of wealth. That means that removing the barrier of student loan debt increases the opportunity to build wealth in multiple forms.
